subject: math

objective.text: Use grid paper to create designs to develop spatial structuring.

source_ref.section: Lesson objective

explanations.title: A design is like an array
explanations.text: A tile design on a grid has rows and columns. You can describe it like an array. Look at the colours in each row.

source_ref.section: Concept Development (S: It looks like an array with 3 rows and 3 columns)

explanations.title: Core unit
explanations.text: A 3 by 3 design has 3 rows and 3 columns. That is 9 squares. We call it a core unit.

source_ref.section: Concept Development Part 4

explanations.title: Tessellation
explanations.text: A tessellation repeats the core unit again and again. The copies touch but do not overlap. There are no gaps. This is also called tiling.

source_ref.section: Concept Development Part 4

explanations.title: Square cut in half
explanations.text: Cut a square in half corner to corner. You get two triangles.

source_ref.section: Concept Development Part 1

explanations.title: Get to the next ten
explanations.text: 9 cents plus 1 cent makes 1 dime. A dime is 10 cents.

Copies touch with no gaps and no overlaps
A design can use a square cut into two triangles

muffin pan 4 columns of 3 with 3 filled

visual_generation_rules: Diffusion cannot count reliably. Any picture where an exact number of objects matters must be built by code (SVG or widget) or drawn by an artist.
Diffusion is allowed only for: style or background art, and single icons (one ball, one pencil, one leaf, one character) that code then tiles to the exact count.
Every visual must be checked by a person: the count shown must equal the stimulus in the question and the rubric answer key.
Animations are described as frames with exact counts per frame, so they can be built or generated and then checked frame by frame.
Visual explanations are valid only when the asset exists (pipeline doc, Planner rules).
